Petition under Sec.34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 seeking setting aside the arbitral award passed by the Learned Sole Arbitrator in A.C.No.174/2024 dated 28.04.2025.
Com AP 110/ 2025 Parties are referred as per their rank before the Arbitral Tribunal.

2. Facts in brief is as under:-
The claimant is into the business of civil constructions.

Karnataka Neeravari Nigam Limited (KNNL) had awarded the work for construction of Samudaya Bhavan in different temples of Sorabha Taluk, Shimoga District covered under package No.57 for a total value of Rs.2,13,32,326/-.
The respondent had entered into an agreement with KNNL for the purpose of undertaking the said work.

The claimant having the required infrastructure, manpower, equipment and financial capacity had entered into a work contract agreement dated 25.11.2020 with the respondent undertaking to execute the work of package No.57 as per the contract document issued by KNNL.

As per the terms of the agreement the payment was to be made by KNNL to the respondent and respondent after retaining 10% of the value of the work done was required to transfer the balance 90% to the claimant after adjusting the recoveries if any under the bills.
The claimant was also required to submit certified GST bills with necessary documents for the work done.

It is submitted that the claimant as per the work order Com AP 110/ 2025 agreement completed the works for gross value of Rs.52,30,654/- under RAB No.1 and at the request of the respondent the claimant raised for an invoice of Rs.41,00,000/- dated 19.03.2021 and was required to raise the invoice for balance amount of Rs.11,30,654/-
after receipt of the amount from KNNL.
It is submitted that even after receiving payment from KNNL the respondent paid only a sum of Rs.16,95,000/- as against RAB No.1 leaving an outstanding amount of Rs.35,35,654/- to be payable.

3. Before arbitrator the respondent filed statement of defence making complete denial of the claim of the claimant.

The respondent admitted having handed over the work under agreement dated 25.11.2020 to the claimant and contended that as per the agreement the claimant was required to complete the work within 5 calender months from the date of agreement and as the claimants failed to complete the said work within the stipulated period and was seeking release of amounts without even starting the work or making any substantial progress in the construction.

It is submitted that as the claimant failed to undertake substantive work as agreed the respondent through email dated 14.12.2021 terminated the work contract for which the Com AP 110/ 2025 claimant sent a notice demanding payment of Rs.38,01,434/- to which a suitable reply came to be issued by the respondent.

It is submitted that during the course of the work the claimant had employed M/s GRSK Constructions, M/s Balaji Agencies and one Mr. Rudrappa Kammanahalli to whom there were amounts due payable to an extent of Rs.24,63,000/- which came to be paid by the respondent.
It is submitted that as the claimant failed to provide NOC from the local labourers and the material suppliers for release of the balance payment the same has been withheld.

It is submitted that under the package No.57 the respondent in all has paid a sum of Rs.21,25,000/- and the claimant is only entitled for the sum of Rs.11,54,571/- out of Rs.41,00,000/- as claimed which is subject to producing the required documents.

It is submitted that the claimant is also required to reimburse a sum of Rs.2,19,624/- for the GST payments and with interest t he claimant is liable to pay a sum of Rs.4,39,286/- towards GST in all a sum of Rs.6,58,610/-.
Deducting the said amount the only amount payable to the claimant is Rs.4,95,661/- which is subject to producing the required documents.

5. Aggrieved by the award passed by the learned sole arbitrator the respondent is before this Court contending that the award passed by the learned sole arbitrator is contrary the pleadings, oral and documentary evidence.

It is submitted that the learned sole arbitrator has not at all taken into consideration the amounts that has been paid totally amounting to Rs.36,93,910/- being already paid and therefore there Com AP 110/ 2025 arose no liability to pay the amount claimed by the claimant.

It is submitted that the learned sole arbitrator has placed much reliance upon Ex.P.4 and P.5 which are nothing but self serving statements prepared at the behest of the site engineer without being duly certified by any competent person and that the learned sole arbitrator has awarded the claim without proper appreciation of the evidence and without taking into consideration the documents at Ex.P.6, P.27 and P.14.

It is submitted that the learned sole arbitrator has failed to appreciate that time was the essence of the contract and as the work was not completed within the stipulated time the respondent was entitled to terminate the contract and therefore no liability arose on the respondent to make any payment.
It is submitted that the arbitrator has failed to consider the fact that the agreement stood terminated on lapse of the time fixed and therefore no liability accrues.

Further it is contended that the learned sole arbitrator has not at all taken into consideration the documents at Ex.D.24, D.26, D.27 and also the evidence of DW-2 and the documents at Ex.D.28 and on these grounds it is contended that the award passed is by ignoring the vital evidence which is an error apparent on face of record and perverse and sought for setting aside the same.

The claimant has filed his statement of objections denying the grounds urged in the petition and has contended that none of the grounds put forth by the petitioner qualify to be accepted as ground for challenge to the award as contemplated under Sec.34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996.

It is contended that the respondent is virtually seeking re- appreciation of evidence which is not permissible under Sec.34 and he is seeking for a review of the judgment which is also not permissible under Sec.34 of the Act.

It is submitted that the award passed by the learned sole arbitrator is upon proper appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence placed on record and therefore no grounds exists whatsoever to interfere with the said award and sought for rejecting the petition with costs.

To put it in nut shell the grounds for challenging the award is that the respondent is virtually asking the Court to re appreciate the evidence that according to the respondent has not been properly evaluated.

11. It is pertinent to mention here that it is now a settled position of law that in a Sec.34 petition the Court cannot undertake the exercise of either review on the merits or re-appreciation of evidence.

The Court can only set aside the award where it is apparently seem to be illegal on face of it or there is perversity in the manner that the learned sole arbitrator has totally ignored the terms of contract has not at all considered the evidence placed before him or has ignored a vital evidence and where the award is passed in blatant breach of any provision of law.
It has been made clear in number of decisions that under Sec.34 the Court cannot do a review on merits nor undertake the exercise of re appreciating the evidence.

In Associate Builders, this Court held that an award could be said to be against the public policy of India in, inter alia, the following circumstances:
42.1. When an award is, on its face, in patent violation of a statutory provision.

42.3. When an award is in violation of the principles of natural justice.
42.4. When an award is unreasonable or perverse.

42.6. When an award is contrary to the interest of India, or against justice or morality, in the sense that it shocks the conscience of the Court."

sentences.text: Interference would be so warranted when award is in violation of 'public policy of India', which has been held to mean 'fundamental policy of Indian law'.
A judicial intervention on account of interfering on merits of award would not be permissible.
However, principles of natural justice as contained in S.18 and 34(2)(a)(iii) of Act would continue to be grounds of challenge of an award.
Ground for interference on basis that award is in conflict with justice or morality is now to be Com AP 110/ 2025 understood as a conflict with 'most basic notions of morality or justice'.

It is only such arbitral awards that shock conscience of Court,
that can be set aside on said ground.
An award would be set aside on ground of patent illegality appearing on ace of award and as such, which goes to roots of matter.

sentences.text: (i) A person deprived of the use of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be compensated for the deprivation, call it by any name.
It may be called interest, compensation or damages.
This basic consideration is as valid for the period the dispute is pending before the arbitrator as it is for the period prior to the arbitrator entering upon the reference.
This is the Com AP 110/ 2025 principle of Section 34, Civil Procedure Code and there is no reason or principle to hold otherwise in the case of arbitrator.
(ii) An arbitrator is an alternative forum for resolution of disputes arising between the parties.
If so, he must have the power to decide all the disputes or differences arising between the parties.

If the arbitrator has no power to award interest pendente lite, the party claiming it would have to approach the court for that purpose, even though he may have obtained satisfaction in respect of other claims from the arbitrator.
This would lead to multiplicity of proceedings.
(iii) An arbitrator is the creature of an agreement.
It is open to the parties to confer upon him such powers and prescribe such procedure for him to follow, as they think fit, so long as they are not opposed to law.
(The proviso to section 41 and Section 3 of Arbitration Act illustrate this point).
The arbitrator must also act and make his award in accordance with the general law of the land and the agreement.

(iv) Over the years, the English and Indian courts have acted on the assumption that where the agreement does not prohibit and a party to the reference makes a claim for interest, the arbitrator must have the power to award interest pendente lite, towards has not been followed in the later decisions of this court.
It has been explained and distinguished on the basis that in that case there was no claim for interest but only a claim for unliquidated damages.
It has been said repeatedly that observations in the said judgment were not intended to lay down any such absolute or universal rule as they appear to, on Com AP 110/ 2025 first impression.
Until Jena case almost all the courts in the country had upheld the power of the arbitrator to award interest pendente lite.
Continuity and certainty is a high desirable feature of law.

sentences.text: In so far as the contentions regarding the respondent having settled the bills Com AP 110/ 2025 towards M/s GRSK Constructions to the tune of Rs,15,53,000/- absolutely no evidence is led before the learned arbitrator.
There is no document or any witnesses examined to infer that the amount of Rs.15,53,000/- which was required to be paid by the claimant has been in fact paid by the respondent.
The statement made in defence to that extent has remained totally unsupported by any cogent and satisfactory evidence.

The learned sole arbitrator at para 17 of the award has undertaken a detailed analysis of the evidence of DW-2 with regards to the amounts payable by him and has come to the conclusion that no cogent evidence is before the Court to infer that DW-2 had the knowledge of construction work and he had undertaken construction of Anganawadi and school buildings.
Whereas on the other hand it is brought out in his evidence that he is only an agriculturist.

The learned arbitrator has also considered the bank statement at Ex.D.31 which only discloses DW-2 having received a sum of Rs.2,30,000/- from the respondent but it does not in any manner indicate that it was amount which was due by the claimant to DW-2.
Thus there is no satisfactory evidence to show that the respondent had paid the amount of Rs.2,30,000/- which was due to be payable by the claimant to DW-2.

Further as regards Com AP 110/ 2025 the amount of Rs.2,00,000/- received by DW-2 reliance is placed upon Ex.D.29 which is in the form of a receipt or payment voucher and on going through the said document there are numerous over writings the amount is written in the words as rupees two lakhs fifty thousand whereas the figures indicate a different amount and the signatures are also not proper there is another receipt at Ex.D.30 which carries altogether a different signature and therefore there is no evidence to infer that the amount of Rs.50,000/- is paid by way of cash in addition Rs.2,00,000/- paid under Ex.P.29 to DW- 2.

The respondent has also examined one witness DW-3 the proprietor of M/s Balaji Agencies who has only deposed to the extent that he has supplied steel worth Rs.7,00,000/- and further his evidence discloses that there is receipt of the entire amount for the value of steel that has been supplied.
DW-3 has deposed in the evidence that he has received Rs.4,30,502/- in cash from the respondent which is not substantiated by any cogent and satisfactory evidence.

Therefore considering these evidences the learned sole arbitrator has come to the conclusion that there is only evidence regarding payment of a sum of Rs.16,95,000/- and respondent is still due in a sum of Rs.35,35,654/- and there is also no evidence to show that the respondent has paid sum of Com AP 110/ 2025 Rs.21,25,000/- as contended.
Thus it is amply clear that the learned sole arbitrator has undertaken a diligent and proper appreciation of the evidence on record.

One of the argument that has been put forth by the respondent is that the learned sole arbitrator has not appreciated that time was the essence of the contract and as the claimant had failed to to any substantial work in the time frame the respondent was justified in terminating the contract and therefore no liability would accrue to make any payments.

It is pertinent to mention here that upon going through the evidence before the learned arbitrator it is clear that under the terms of the work agreement at Ex.P.1 there is no scope of unilateral termination of the contract.

Moreover the termination notice which is at Ex.D.17 has never been acted upon the parties because even after issuance of notice subsequent conducts have taken place and the contention of the respondent that he had made payments not only to the claimant but also to DW-2 and 3 on behalf of the claimant are all subsequent to the issuance of notice of termination.

sentences.text: Yet another argument that was put forth by the respondent was that it is only due in a sum of Rs.11,54,571/- with respect to which there is sought for a deduction of sum of Rs.6,58,910/- towards GST and the balance if any payable is only Rs.4,95,661/- which is subject to production of certain documents.
This contention again urged in the statement of defence has remained totally unsubstantiated in course of trial before the arbitral proceedings.
The respondent has not lead any acceptable evidence before the arbitrator to draw an inference that the amount payable by the respondent is only Rs.4,95,661/-.

On the other hand the claimant thorough his evidence has been successful in proving its case and therefore the leaned arbitrator concluding that the respondent is liable to pay a sum of Rs.40,77,654/- with current and future interest at 10% p.a. on Rs.27,62,480/-
is based upon proper and well reasoned appreciation of the evidence and therefore the award is neither oppose to any public policy nor is in contravention of any rules and regulations nor there is any patent illegality appearing on the face of it or Com AP 110/ 2025 perversity requiring this Court to interfere and set aside the same.

Thus it can be held without hesitation that the respondent has hopelessly failed in substantiating the grounds that has been urged for setting aside the award and hence, I answer Point No.1 in the Negative.

The Court can only set aside the award where it is apparently seem to be illegal on face of it or there is perversity in the manner that the learned sole arbitrator has totally ignored the terms of contract has not at all considered the evidence placed before him or has ignored a vital evidence and where the award is passed in blatant breach of any provision of law.
The position regarding power of Court to set aside arbitral award can be summarised thus:
(1) The Court can set aside the arbitral award under Section 34(2) of the Act if the party making the application furnishes proof that:-(i) a party was under some incapacity, or(ii) the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it or, failing any indication thereon, under the law for the time being in force;
or(iii) the party making the application was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case; or(iv) the arbitral award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration, or it contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration;
